## Week 1
#### Readings
* [Chapple (2017) "Income Inequality and Urban Displacement: The New Gentrification"](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/6rb5b8bd) (10 pp.) — the argument that frames the course: focus on *displacement*, not just gentrification, and treat it as an *income* crisis, not only a housing one.

#### Tuesday July 7 - Lecture
* Course introduction and [syllabus](syllabus.qmd)
* How to use AI in this course - discussion and live demo

#### Thursday July 9 - Lab
* Lab 1: getting started in RStudio on the DataHub (we walk through it together online), intro to R, and your first Census number
* AI tutorial: debugging with AI, verifying answers, and sharing your conversation link

#### Set up this week
* Get a free census API key at <https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html> (a couple minutes). The key arrives by email — **click the activation link in that email**, or the key won't work in lab.
* Set up a free account on an AI assistant that can share a public conversation link (Perplexity recommended; ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude also work). Sign in with a **personal** account, not your CalNet login, so that link-sharing works. [See the AI policy for details.](syllabus.html#ai-policy)

#### Thursday July 16 - Lab

## Week 3
#### Readings
***Due before lab, Thursday July 23***

* [Walker (2023) Chapter 3](https://walker-data.com/census-r/wrangling-census-data-with-tidyverse-tools.html) & [Chapter 4](https://walker-data.com/census-r/exploring-us-census-data-with-visualization.html) — chapter 3 is lab 3's wrangling verbs (filter/mutate/group_by, margins of error); chapter 4 is its charts. Read them behind the lab and everything clicks twice.

#### Tuesday July 21 - Lab

* Warm-up tour in [Social Explorer](https://www.socialexplorer.com/): how census geographies nest — states, counties, tracts, block groups, blocks — and what size each polygon really is

* Reading Census tables like a researcher: dollars vs. counts and the universe rule, hunting down table B25070 in the catalog yourself, census-tract neighborhoods, and reshaping with `pivot_wider()` — the skills Assignment 2's build-a-measure asks for

#### Thursday July 23 - Lab

* Lab 3, part B — picking up at section 7: charts, done right. Which plot answers which question — bar, histogram, boxplot, scatter, and the chart-picker card — with the [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://opensource.posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/data-visualization/) at your elbow, plus summarizing with `group_by()` + `summarize()`

#### **Assignment 1** - *Due Monday, July 27 @5pm*

A short solo warm-up, and the first step of a thread you carry through Assignment 2 and your final project. Pick a county, set of counties, or region you care about - you will keep working with this same area all term.

1. Use `get_acs()` to pull one ACS variable that says something about housing precarity (for example, rent burden, median rent, or the share of households that rent).
2. Make one chart of it (a bar chart across your counties works well).
3. Write two or three sentences describing what the chart shows and anything that surprised you.

Submit your R script, the chart, your sentences, and the share link(s) to any AI you used. Keep it simple - no bibliography or ASA formatting needed yet. Submit to bCourses.

## Week 5

#### **Assignment 2** - *Due Monday, August 3 @5pm*

Build directly on Assignment 1: stay with the same area and go deeper. This becomes the seed of your final group project.

Add two or three more ACS variables and combine them into a measure of displacement risk, inequality, or some other housing precarity measure using the American Community Survey. Include descriptive statistics, plots, and an interpretation of what you found. End with a draft research question and at least two hypotheses you could test about the disparate impact of displacement in your area. Submit to bCourses.

For this assignment you will submit:

1. R code script that is replicable by the grader,

2. a brief writeup explaining your assignment with plots and context,
    * Include one or more introductory paragraphs summarizing what you are analyzing and your overall findings.
    * Text and plots walking the reader through a more detailed understanding of what you found. Make sure to describe your plots.
    * A draft research question and at least two hypotheses for your final project.

3. Bibliography and inline citations in ASA (American Sociological Association) format.

4. List of URL links to any and all AI usage (use any approved AI tool that can share a public conversation link).
    * In your code, put the URL in comments next to the relevant area.
    * In your writeup, put the URL in footnotes near the section or text in which you used AI. [See AI policy in the Syllabus for more info.](syllabus.html#ai-policy)


These assignments will be graded on the [scale in the syllabus](syllabus.html#course-grading). This grade is to help you see the quality of your work but the final grade will be graded as complete or incomplete. No late assignments will be accepted except for special accommodations. You can volunteer to present a 5-minute demo of your assignment in class.

Your draft research question and hypotheses do double duty. Group formation happens in class on Tuesday August 4, and your group's project pitch starts from what each member drafted here.

As with Assignment 1, there is a complete worked example to learn from: `code/a2_example.R` (on the [DataHub](https://r.datahub.berkeley.edu/hub/user-redirect/git-pull?repo=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fevictionresearch%2FSOC-N100-Housing-Precarity-2026&urlpath=rstudio%2F)) picks up exactly where the A1 example left off: same five Washington counties, now at the census-tract level, with three new ACS tables combined into a simple precarity score. It also models the parts that are new in A2 - the writeup structure, the research question and hypotheses, ASA citations, and AI links - and closes with an optional lab-4-style tract map of the score. Read it for the shape, then build your own for your area.

#### Tuesday August 4 - Lecture + final project groups

*First hour - lecture: what actually helps.* The research-to-policy story behind everything you have built so far:

* How eviction data becomes policy, and why most states still cannot see their own eviction crisis
* Watch in class: Tim's testimony to the Washington State Senate ([slides](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1x7SCdTeBdczY5Ga5wvixMxtvTv-a4rTph6LIQWLsIk0/edit?pli=1&slide=id.g32100058b3b_1_1#slide=id.g32100058b3b_1_1) | [recording, starts at 40 minutes](https://tvw.org/video/senate-housing-2024121118/)) - a complex story told simply with data, and the model for your final presentation

*Second hour - final project groups:*

#### Thursday August 6 - Lab

* Lab 5, our last teaching lab: measure neighborhood racial segregation with ERN's `neighborhood` package, join it to the Lab 3 rent-burden measure, and test whether the two move together - with side-by-side (dodged) bar charts, a brief on migration data (ACS table B07004, who moved IN by race, and what changes when you ask it about tracts instead of counties), mapping where the Black-Latine neighborhoods are and how fast White residents are arriving in them, interactive tmaps of where each group is moving in, a diverging map of where White arrival outpaces Black arrival and where it does not, plus an optional look at the county-only data that does count who moved out, and pulling an outside dataset off a state agency's website (`code/lab5_rb_seg.R` on the [DataHub](https://r.datahub.berkeley.edu/hub/user-redirect/git-pull?repo=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fevictionresearch%2FSOC-N100-Housing-Precarity-2026&urlpath=rstudio%2F))
* Bonus self-study for the final project: reading a real risk model, the Housing Precarity Risk Model (`code/lab6_hprm.R`, same DataHub link) - every census tract in the country scored 0 to 8, split into its displacement and eviction channels, plus the rent gap, the eviction clock, and how the model's answer compares with the rent-burden measure you built yourself. A short path uses only verbs from Labs 1 to 3; a long path goes further. We will not walk through it in class

## Research Opportunities

If this class made you want to keep doing this kind of work, two Berkeley programs are worth a look. Both give you academic credit rather than pay, and both have Fall 2026 deadlines that land right after this course ends, so now is the time to look.

* [**Data Discovery**](https://cdss.berkeley.edu/discovery), run by the College of Computing, Data Science, and Society, puts students on research teams working with academic, government, nonprofit, and industry partners. This is the more technical of the two and the closer match to what we have been doing in lab, so if the coding side of this class is what grabbed you, start here. You earn three units, the commitment is about 9 hours a week, and you present a poster at a symposium during RRR week. For Fall 2026, projects post **August 10** and **applications close August 21**. Note that it includes a weekly in-person Tuesday meeting, which matters if you are not going to be in Berkeley this fall.

* [**URAP**](https://research.berkeley.edu/urap/), the Undergraduate Research Apprentice Program, pairs you directly with a faculty member or research staff on their project. It is much broader than Data Discovery and spans the full range of social science topics, so it is the better entry point if you want research experience without a heavy technical requirement. You earn 1 unit for every 3 hours of work a week, up to 4 units a term, on one project per semester. **Fall 2026 applications open August 21.**

One eligibility catch worth checking before you invest time in an application. Both programs are for enrolled Berkeley undergraduates, and neither accepts concurrent enrollment or visiting students. If you are taking this course through Summer Sessions without being a matriculated Berkeley student, confirm your status with the program before applying.

Happy to talk through which one fits what you want to do, or to write you a reference. Just email me.
